channel.description: Archive records from the View from Nowhere (10s) era
channel.generator: Jay Rosen Digital Archive RSS Generator

item.title: A call for radically different campaign coverage
item.description: Rosen and Brandel call on newsrooms to adopt a 'citizens agenda' model for campaign coverage, centering voters' information needs rather than horse race narratives. They announce a partnership between Hearken and the Membership Puzzle Project to support newsrooms willing to rethink election coverage.

item.title: Is your organization thinking about membership? Take some ideas and maybe some money from the Membership Puzzle Project
item.description: Nieman Lab profiles the Membership Puzzle Project's work helping news organizations develop membership models. The project, led by Rosen and based at NYU, provided research, case studies, and grants through the Membership in News Fund. The article highlights the Daily Maverick in South Africa as a success story, with 6,200 members in nine months covering 20% of costs.

item.title: The Correspondent's editor-in-chief talks about what U.S. expansion means and doesn't
item.description: Nieman Lab interviews The Correspondent's editor-in-chief Rob Wijnberg about the confusion surrounding their U.S. expansion. After raising $2.5 million with ambassadors including Rosen and Nate Silver, the site announced it would remain headquartered in Amsterdam rather than opening a U.S. newsroom. Rosen acknowledged the confusion was the company's fault due to earlier messaging, while Wijnberg defended their global-first approach.

item.title: Stand Up! with Pete Dominick: Episode 861 - Journalism Professor Jay Rosen
item.description: Rosen appears on Pete Dominick's podcast to discuss journalism, media criticism, and the state of public conversation in America. The wide-ranging interview covers Rosen's key ideas about press reform and the challenges facing journalism.

item.title: Speaking the hard truth to journalism (Center for Media at Risk podcast)
item.description: The Center for Media at Risk podcast features Rosen discussing the hard truths facing journalism, including the profession's reluctance to acknowledge its own role in the current crisis and the structural challenges that make reform so difficult.

item.title: A roundup of trends that are changing journalism
item.description: A syllabus-style overview of 21 trends reshaping journalism, developed for Rosen's NYU 'digital thinking' class. Covers social media as distribution, mobile shift, new business models (data, events, native ads, nonprofit, crowdfunding), analytics, product focus, UX design, data journalism, structured data, personalization, transparency, open journalism, automation, agile newsrooms, personal franchise model, niche journalism, explainer journalism, news as service, curation, fact-checking, and platform power. Originally from PressThink, republished on IJNet.

item.title: The public service veto: How The Correspondent protects itself from profit maximization
item.description: As Trust Advisor to The Correspondent, Rosen explains the legal structure that prevents the member-funded news site from being sold to a profit-maximizing company. He details how a Dutch foundation, SDM, holds a 'priority share' that acts as a public service veto over changes to the site's founding principles, including its 5% profit cap and ad-free model.

item.title: What The Correspondent will add to the American press
item.description: Rosen explains his decision to work with De Correspondent on its English-language expansion, describing it as a response to the deep structural problems in American journalism exposed by 2016. He details the site's seven key features -- no ads, member-funded, no meter, escape from the news cycle, revised editorial contracts, knowledge exchange with readers, and no 'view from nowhere' -- arguing the model reconfigures how a public stands toward journalists.

item.title: Center for Media at Risk launch symposium
item.description: Event page for the Center for Media at Risk launch symposium at the University of Pennsylvania's Annenberg School, featuring a panel with Amy Siskind, Jay Rosen, and Leah Wright Rigueur discussing threats to journalism and democracy.

item.title: Optimizing journalism for trust
item.description: Rosen argues that news organizations should be optimized for trust rather than clicks or scoops, proposing that trust must be designed into journalism. He unpacks what 'optimizing for trust' means in practice, from transparent data policies to showing your work, and explains why he is helping De Correspondent expand to English-language publishing.

item.title: Jay Rosen (ONA17 speaker profile)
item.description: Speaker profile page for Rosen at the 2017 Online News Association conference, where he participated in discussions about digital journalism, press criticism, and the future of news in the Trump era.

item.title: What are journalists for in the age of Trump?
item.description: A brief write-up of a conversation between Jay Rosen and journalist Kathy Kiely at the Uncharted Festival of Ideas in Berkeley about the right frame for interpreting press coverage during the Trump presidency. The article accompanies an audio recording of their discussion about journalism's role and responsibilities.

item.title: Is trust-based journalism the future? Jay Rosen thinks so
item.description: Dan Kennedy at GBH profiles Rosen's argument that trust-based journalism represents the future of the industry. The piece discusses Rosen's work with De Correspondent and his broader thesis that news organizations must design their operations around earning and maintaining public trust.

item.title: Jay Rosen: This is what a news organization built on reader trust looks like
item.description: Rosen explains why De Correspondent, a Dutch member-funded news site, represents what a trust-optimized news organization looks like. He describes its ad-free model, freedom from the 24-hour news cycle, writer-centered structure, and journalist-as-discussion-leader approach, then announces the Membership Puzzle Project and his role as ambassador for The Correspondent's U.S. expansion.

item.title: NYU to launch Membership Puzzle Project
item.description: Knight Foundation announces $515,000 in funding from Knight, First Look Media, and Democracy Fund for the Membership Puzzle Project at NYU, led by Rosen, working with Dutch news startup De Correspondent. The project aims to bring De Correspondent's membership model to the United States and research how membership can advance sustainability and trust in journalism.

item.title: NYU Journalism launches Membership Puzzle Project led by Prof. Jay Rosen
item.description: NYU Journalism announces the launch of the Membership Puzzle Project, a research initiative led by Rosen to study how membership models can sustain journalism and build trust. The project, funded by Knight Foundation and others, will research membership-driven news organizations worldwide.

item.title: After the Agora: Jay Rosen: Rebuilding trust in media
item.description: Texas A&M University announces Rosen's lecture in its 'After the Agora' series, where he discusses rebuilding trust in media and the challenges facing the public sphere in the digital age.

item.title: Jay Rosen on the hazards of journalism-as-usual under the Trump administration
item.description: Rosen discusses with Poynter's Benjamin Mullin the collapsing notion of the White House spokesperson, how to cover Trump's tweets, why news organizations should send the interns to the briefing room, and journalism's tendency to stay the same. He argues that routines from previous administrations no longer apply and that the White House Correspondents' Dinner should become an unconference about covering the Trump White House.

item.title: Full transcript: Jay Rosen on Recode Media
item.description: Extended transcript of Rosen's interview with Peter Kafka covering the press under Trump. Rosen discusses threat modeling for press freedom, the weakening of reality as a constraint in politics, why journalists should stop interviewing Kellyanne Conway without journalistic rationale, and the lessons of David Fahrenthold's transparent reporting methods.

item.title: Maximize trust: Jay Rosen on covering the Trump administration
item.description: Vermont Public Radio interviews Rosen about his advice for journalists covering the Trump administration. Rosen argues that maximizing trust, not just producing scoops, should be the press's primary strategic goal when facing a president who actively works to discredit journalism.

item.title: Jay Rosen addresses journalism's changing landscape
item.description: Saint Michael's College reports on Rosen's lecture about journalism's changing landscape, titled 'What We Need From Journalists Now That Trump Has Been Elected,' delivered to the college community.

item.title: New reality (On the Media episode)
item.description: A full On the Media episode featuring Rosen on Trump-era journalism, exploring how the new political reality requires the press to fundamentally rethink its assumptions, practices, and relationship with a president who actively works to undermine factual discourse.

item.title: How the press can save itself in the age of Trump (Recode Media podcast)
item.description: Rosen discusses with Peter Kafka how the press can survive and remain effective in the Trump era. He outlines strategies including threat modeling, shifting from the view from nowhere, and learning from David Fahrenthold's transparent reporting methods.

item.title: Journalists should stop interviewing Kellyanne Conway (Recode Media clip)
item.description: A clip from the Recode Media podcast where Rosen argues that journalists should stop interviewing Kellyanne Conway because the journalistic rationale for booking her has evaporated -- she doesn't reliably represent Trump's positions and her interviews leave viewers more confused than before.

item.title: Why the view from nowhere is a harmful myth
item.description: On the Media features Rosen explaining why 'the view from nowhere' -- journalism's claim to a God's-eye objectivity -- is a harmful myth that undermines trust and prevents reporters from telling audiences what they actually know to be true.

item.title: NYU and De Correspondent launch new laboratory for community supported investigative news
item.description: Josh Stearns reports on the launch of the Membership Puzzle Project, a joint initiative between NYU and De Correspondent led by Rosen, which serves as a research laboratory for studying how community-supported models can sustain investigative journalism.

item.title: Jay Rosen on the view from nowhere
item.description: Stowe Boyd discusses and amplifies Rosen's concept of 'the view from nowhere,' explaining how journalism's claim to objectivity masks real ideological choices and why this matters more than ever in the Trump era.

item.title: The thin legitimacy of social media as a news source
item.description: In PBS NewsHour's Brief But Spectacular series, Rosen discusses the 'thin legitimacy' of Facebook as a news platform, distinguishing between thin and thick legitimacy in how platforms relate to users. He argues that choosing serious journalism is connected to the choice to continue being a democracy.

item.title: Brief but Spectacular: Jay Rosen on the state of journalism in the age of Facebook
item.description: Full transcript of Rosen's PBS Brief But Spectacular segment. He discusses how making media has become easier while getting people to read serious journalism has become harder. He introduces the concepts of 'thin legitimacy' (Facebook's terms of service) versus 'thick legitimacy' (genuine trust), and argues that choosing serious journalism is connected to choosing democracy.

item.title: Media critic Jay Rosen on 2016 campaign coverage and the rise of Trump: "That's the way authoritarian societies work"
item.description: Paul Rosenberg interviews Jay Rosen about his six-point framework for what the campaign press should not be neutral toward: participation, verification, deliberation, accountability, transparency (against opacity), and demagoguery. Rosen argues these values are already latent in journalism and need to be made explicit in an era of authoritarian politics.

item.title: Civic journalism, engaged journalism: Tracing the connections
item.description: Geneva Overholser traces the connections between the 1990s civic journalism movement and the 2010s engaged journalism practices for the Democracy Fund. She argues that while civic journalism was resisted by newsrooms in the 1990s (only 7% of AP managing editors strongly agreed with it), its core principle of richer conversation with audiences has come into widespread practice. The piece positions engaged journalism as a 'much-evolved descendant' of civic journalism.

item.title: Donald Trump is crashing the system. Journalists need to build a new one.
item.description: Rosen argues that Trump's candidacy upends the assumptions underlying campaign journalism -- from the seriousness of policy proposals to the shaming effect of fact-checking. He urges journalists to recognize that normal rules don't apply and to develop novel, less predictable responses to an 'unbound' candidate who exploits and crashes the conventions of political reporting.

item.title: Jay Rosen's NYU students dig deeper into disruption of news business
item.description: MediaShift reports on Studio 20 students at NYU, under Rosen's direction, researching the disruption of the news business. The piece highlights student projects examining new models for journalism sustainability and innovation.

item.title: The Pub #62: Jay Rosen on his love-hate relationship with public media
item.description: Current's The Pub podcast features Rosen discussing his complicated relationship with public media. He is famous for applying 'the view from nowhere' to NPR's impartial journalism but calls himself 'a total fan of public radio' and a 'loyal critic.' He criticizes NPR reporters for covering controversies without trying to discover which side is right, which he says is different from arbitrating who is right.

item.title: Tech is eating media
item.description: Rosen responds to John Herrman's essay on how the tech industry is absorbing the press. He argues that tech platforms may end up ingesting journalism without owning the problem of keeping real journalism going, and calls for more companies willing to take on the headache of editorial responsibility.

item.title: Misinterpreting Williams' misremembering
item.description: Article discusses the Brian Williams controversy over false reporting and mentions Jay Rosen in relation to media credibility issues. The piece appears to reference Rosen's commentary on the Williams situation.

item.title: Journalism Professor Rosen on changing nature of news
item.description: Saint Michael's College announces a lecture by Rosen on the changing nature of news, part of the college's ongoing engagement with questions about journalism, democracy, and media evolution.

item.title: NYU professor Jay Rosen's roadmap for understanding the media landscape
item.description: Bleacher Report covers Rosen's framework for understanding the changing media landscape, likely from a talk or presentation he gave about the forces reshaping news and the digital media environment.

item.title: Journalists need a point of view if they want to stay relevant
item.description: Rosen argues that extreme political polarization has made traditional journalistic objectivity obsolete. He contends that newsrooms should hire reporters with transparent points of view, call out falsehoods rather than hiding behind balance, and adopt accountability journalism models like ProPublica's -- or risk sliding into irrelevance.

item.title: Blogging and the new public intellectual
item.description: Rosen and Megan Garber discuss how blogging created a new form of public intellectual engagement, one that bypasses traditional academic and media gatekeepers. Published by the Hannah Arendt Center at Bard College, the piece connects blogging to Arendt's ideas about public life and thinking in the open.

item.title: ISOJ 2014/2019 speaker: Jay Rosen
item.description: Speaker profile for Rosen at the International Symposium on Online Journalism (ISOJ), where he participated in both the 2014 and 2019 editions of the conference discussing online journalism, digital media, and press reform.

item.title: A first look at NewCo's business, journalism structure
item.description: Rosen examines the business and editorial structure of Pierre Omidyar's First Look Media, analyzing its dual structure of a for-profit tech company and a nonprofit journalism organization. The piece, syndicated from PressThink, discusses what Omidyar's venture means for investigative journalism.

item.title: Jay Rosen, the view from nowhere, and 'arrogance born of monopoly'
item.description: Nieman Lab highlights Rosen's PressThink blog post using the Old and New Testaments as a framework for discussing the age of mass media. Rosen argues that journalism's 'new testament fundamentalism' -- its rigid objectivity -- was 'arrogance born of monopoly' that is now giving way as journalists begin blogging, using social media, and recognizing that their business model is broken.

item.title: Summer reading 2013: Getting the connections right
item.description: Nieman Lab excerpts Rosen's 1996 book 'Getting the Connections Right' as part of its Summer Reading series. The excerpt contrasts journalism's obsession with 'getting the separations right' (editorial vs. business, facts vs. values, news vs. opinion) with Rosen's argument that the deeper challenge is getting the connections right -- between journalism and the public, between facts and values, between the editorial product and civic life.

item.title: Defining journalists - and their rights
item.description: Article discusses the definition of journalists and their rights in the context of citizen journalism and blogger protections. Mentions Jay Rosen of NYU's journalism program in the context of discussing citizen journalism and how it relates to traditional journalism.

item.title: Press Publish 3: Jay Rosen on the public, how the press thinks, and the production of innocence
item.description: Joshua Benton interviews Rosen for the Nieman Lab Press Publish podcast, covering his entry into journalism academia, the influence of James Carey and Neil Postman, the Lippmann-Dewey debate, the rise and quasi-fall of civic journalism, why horse race journalism needs improvement, and what Rosen calls 'the production of innocence' -- journalism's way of distancing itself from its own role in political outcomes.

item.title: Don't bust bogus "hype"
item.description: Rosen criticizes a Salon article that claimed to bust Reddit and citizen journalism hype after the Aurora shootings but failed to produce any actual evidence of the hype it claimed to debunk. He argues the article is itself a form of hype -- a 'linkless hype buster' that pretends to deflate overblown claims that were never actually made.

item.title: How polarization undermined the press
item.description: A Wonkblog post by Rosen about how political polarization has undermined the press. The original content is no longer available at this URL.

item.title: Jay Rosen on our media malaise: Who will tell the people?
item.description: Rosen joins Christopher Lydon on Open Source Radio to discuss the media malaise in America, the crisis of trust in journalism, and the structural challenges preventing the press from fulfilling its democratic role. The conversation explores who can inform the public when the press itself is under siege.

item.title: Civic journalism 2.0: The Guardian and NYU launch a citizens agenda for 2012
item.description: Nieman Lab covers the launch of a citizens agenda project between The Guardian and NYU's Studio 20, led by Rosen and Amanda Michel. The project applies civic journalism principles to the 2012 election, asking voters what issues matter most rather than following the horse race. Digital First Media partners to tailor findings to local coverage.
